questions.question: Animals must eat to get their food, but green plants make their own, out of water and air, using the energy in sunlight. What is this process called?
questions.context: Photosynthesis is how a plant makes its own food from water and air, powered by sunlight. Pollination carries pollen from flower to flower, germination is a seed sprouting, and transpiration is water leaving a plant's leaves as vapour.
questions.grade_note: NGSS 5-LS1-1 and 5th-grade plant units teach that plants make their own food, and name the process photosynthesis.

questions.question: A plant needs sunlight and water to make its food. It also takes in one thing from the air for the job. What does it take in?
questions.context: A plant joins carbon dioxide from the air with water to make its food. Plants take in some oxygen too, but they use it to break their food down for energy, not to make it. Nitrogen is most of the air but goes into no part of the sugar, and there is barely any hydrogen in the air at all.
questions.grade_note: The 5th-grade line G5.L3 (NGSS 5-LS1-1) teaches that a plant's food and matter come from carbon dioxide in the air and water.

questions.question: A pondweed grows under the water in a glass jar on a sunny windowsill, and tiny bubbles of gas rise from its leaves. Which gas is the pondweed giving off as it makes its food?
questions.context: As the pondweed makes its food in sunlight, its leaves give off oxygen, which rises as bubbles; in the dark the bubbles soon stop. Carbon dioxide is the gas it takes in to make that food, not the one it gives off. The same oxygen from plants is what people and animals breathe.
questions.grade_note: 5th graders learn that plants give off oxygen as they make their food (G5.L3, the scope's 'plants give off oxygen'), and a pondweed's bubbles in sunlight are the standard classroom way to show it (F32).

questions.question: Under the ground, a potato plant grows potatoes packed with stored food. Which part of the plant makes that food in the first place?
questions.context: The leaves make sugar in sunlight, and the sugar travels down the plant to the potatoes, where it is stored as starch. A plant can make food only where light reaches its green parts, and roots and potatoes sit in the dark soil.
questions.grade_note: 5th-grade units (NGSS 5-LS1-1, CK G5 Plant Structures and Processes) teach that a plant makes its food in its leaves.

questions.question: Using the Sun's light, a leaf joins water and carbon dioxide together to make the plant's food. What kind of food does the leaf make?
questions.context: The leaf makes sugar, which feeds the whole plant and can be stored as starch. Minerals and salts come into a plant from the soil and are not made in its leaves, and protein needs nitrogen, which water and carbon dioxide do not contain.
questions.grade_note: The 5th-grade line G5.L3 teaches that leaves make sugar (glucose) as the plant's food.

questions.question: A tiny acorn can grow, over many years, into a huge oak tree. Where does most of the matter that builds the tree come from?
questions.context: A tree builds its wood mostly out of carbon dioxide from the air and water from the ground. The soil gives it only small amounts of minerals, and sunlight gives the energy for the building but none of the matter.
questions.grade_note: NGSS 5-LS1-1 asks 5th graders to argue that plant matter comes mostly from air and water, not from the soil.

questions.question: A cow spends hours every day eating grass, and the grass gives her the energy to walk about and keep warm. How did that energy get into the grass?
choices: It drew it up from the soil
It soaked it up from the rain
It took it in from the air
questions.context: Grass catches energy from sunlight as it makes its food, and stores that energy in its sugar. The soil, the rain and the air give the grass materials to build with, but no energy, so the cow runs on energy that was once the Sun's light.
questions.grade_note: NGSS 5-PS3-1 asks 5th graders to show that the energy in animals' food was once energy from the Sun.

questions.question: The word photosynthesis joins two old Greek words. One of them, synthesis, means putting together. What does the other one, photo, mean?
questions.context: Photo comes from the Greek word for light, so photosynthesis means putting together with light. A photograph is named for the same word, as a drawing made with light. Green and leaf are the Greek roots of chlorophyll, the green substance in leaves.
questions.grade_note: The 5th-grade line G5.L3 itself teaches the word's parts: 'photo' = light, 'synthesis' = putting together.

24bc41fcf8.why: Judge (medium, tell): 'Carbon dioxide' and 'Carbon monoxide' were a sound-alike pair that gave a guesser even odds, and carbon monoxide is not a gas 5th graders are taught. 'Carbon monoxide' is now 'Hydrogen', as the judge proposed (a gas a child ties to water; only about half a part per million of the air, new F33, checked now), and the context says so. With the one long lure gone, the bare 'Carbon dioxide' stood out as the long choice (the length gate's FAIL), so every choice now ends in 'gas' and the stem asks what the plant takes in ('one thing from the air') rather than 'which gas'. 'Water vapour' was not used as the long lure: some air plants (Tillandsia) do absorb water vapour through their leaves, so it would be partly true. Same fact and key (F2).

b73f332c51.why: Judge (medium, tell): the stem asked which gas 'lets the flame burn', answerable from fire knowledge without the plant's fact; judge (medium, other): the candle-and-mint jar is Priestley's experiment, which the T4 unit photosynthesis-atoms-in-and-out owns, so it was the first step of an advanced story. Rewritten, as the judge proposed, on the same fact (a plant gives off oxygen as it makes food, F31): a pondweed's bubbles in sunlight (new F32, checked now: Grokipedia Elodea), with no flame and no named experiment. The stem asks which gas the pondweed gives off as it makes its food, not which gas fills the bubbles, because the bubbles also carry some nitrogen from the water (F32's caution). The lures are carbon dioxide (soda bubbles, M5), nitrogen (most of the air) and water vapour (boiling bubbles, M10).

d37803faca.why: Judge (medium, tell): 'Starch' and 'Nectar' were dead (a white food store; a sweet liquid in flowers), so chlorophyll won by elimination. They are now 'Cellulose' and 'Glucose', as the judge proposed: leaf substances a child cannot rule out by colour or place, the classic confusion of the food with the light-catcher (new M9). Glucose is the sugar this unit teaches (the curriculum line names 'sugar (glucose)'); cellulose is new to the grade, so the context says what it is (new F34, F35, checked now: Grokipedia Cellulose, Glucose). 'Chloroplast' and 'Chlorine' were left out, as the judge warned. Stem and key unchanged.

dropped.question: Many trees' leaves turn from green to yellow and orange in autumn. The green substance that catches sunlight for making food breaks down, and the yellow and orange that were there all along show through. What is the green substance called?
dropped.why: failed the re-check: Grade fit of the new lure 'Cellulose'. No 5th-grade standard teaches the word: NGSS 5-LS1-1, TEKS 5 and Core Knowledge G5 do not name it. It turns up only as an optional extension in a grade 6 (5-7) lesson (TeachEngineering), and the writer's own notes call it 'new to the grade' and 'an unknown leaf word' (M9). A 5th grader cannot weigh it. It is live only as an unfamiliar science-sounding term, not as a confusion the grade really makes (config distractor rule), so a half-sure child who studied the unit is pulled by a word he or she was never taught. 'Glucose' is fair: G5.L3 names 'sugar (glucose)', grade 5-7 lessons teach 'a simple sugar called glucose', and food against light-catcher is the real confusion. The facts are otherwise true: chlorophyll is the green light-absorbing pigment, autumn reveals carotenoids already present, cellulose builds cell walls, and glucose is not green. Fix: replace 'Cellulose' with a leaf word the grade is taught; keep Glucose and Carotene.
